name: Mobility / dispatch surge & ETA features
category: Adjacent — dispatch decision features (ride-hailing, delivery, freight)
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Mobility dispatch — ride-hailing / on-demand delivery / freight matching real-time decision features (surge pricing, driver-courier matching, ETA prediction, restaurant prep-time, route-completion feedback)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A dispatch / pricing / ETA service for a ride-hailing, food-delivery or freight-matching platform decides — within a ~50-300 ms budget on every ride-request, order-creation or driver-offer event — which driver/courier/carrier to dispatch, what surge multiplier to apply, and what ETA to quote, by reading per-(H3 cell × product), per-driver and per-restaurant rolling counters / velocities / distributions of demand, supply, acceptance, cancellation and ETA-error.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Power the surge / primetime / dynamic-pricing controller with per-H3-cell (or per-S2-cell, per-geohash) rolling counts of open ride requests and available drivers over short windows (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 min are Uber Gairos's documented window set) for every active hexagon, so a downstream pricing model can compute a supply/demand ratio and a surge multiplier every few seconds. 2) Score driver/courier offers in real time with per-driver acceptance-rate, cancellation-rate, idle-time, recent-completion-count and ETA-bias features so the dispatch optimizer (DoorDash DeepRed, Uber Marketplace matching, GoJek Jaeger) can pick the best (rider, driver) or (order, dasher) pair beyond raw geographic proximity. 3) Feed the ETA model (Uber DeepETA, DoorDash store-order-count features, Lyft Primetime/Dispatch features) with per-restaurant prep-time velocity, per-route ETA-error feedback and per-(origin × destination × hour-of-day) historic-vs-actual deltas so the platform can quote rider/customer ETAs that match observed reality.
domain_fit.event_shapes: ride_request {ts, rider_id, h3_cell, product_type (UberX/Pool/Comfort), origin_lat_lng, destination_lat_lng}, driver_state {ts, driver_id, h3_cell, status (online/idle/on_trip/offline), product_eligibility}, driver_offer {ts, offer_id, driver_id, request_id, eta_seconds, surge_multiplier}, offer_response {ts, offer_id, accepted_or_declined}, ride_cancel {ts, ride_id, canceller (rider/driver), reason}, ride_complete {ts, ride_id, predicted_eta, actual_duration, distance, route_id, surge_at_quote}. Food-delivery analogue: order_created {ts, order_id, store_id, courier_id_or_null, h3_cell}, store_order_count_event {ts, store_id, queue_depth}, dasher_state {ts, dasher_id, status, h3_cell}, prep_complete {ts, order_id, prep_seconds}, pickup {ts, order_id, dasher_id, wait_at_store_seconds}, dropoff {ts, order_id, eta_at_quote, actual_seconds}. Freight analogue: load_posted {ts, load_id, origin, destination, equipment_type}, carrier_state {ts, carrier_id, dot_id, lat_lng, available_capacity}, bid {ts, load_id, carrier_id, price}, tender_accept / reject. The relevant primary-key shapes — (h3_cell × product), driver_id, store_id, (origin × dest × hour) — are all already supported by beava's @bv.table(key=...) declaration.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: (a) Per-(h3_cell × product) sliding/hopping counts of ride_request, driver_online_state, ride_cancel over (1,2,4,8,16,32) minute windows — Uber Gairos publicly runs exactly this with 9 ring radii × 6 window sizes = 54 features per hex per minute. (b) Per-(h3_cell × product) supply_demand_ratio = count(open_requests)/count(available_drivers) — a derived ratio that pricing reads. (c) Per-driver rolling acceptance_rate = count(accept)/count(offer) over last 50 offers or last 60 min; cancellation_rate over last 24 h; idle_time = time-since-last ride_complete / since-going-online; trips_per_hour velocity. (d) Per-store/restaurant prep_time velocity (rolling avg over last N completed orders or last K min), order_queue_depth count, prep_time_p50/p90 distribution. (e) Per-route or per-(origin × dest × hour-of-day) ETA-error rolling mean and stddev (actual_minus_predicted), fed back to bias-correct the ETA model — the DeeprETA paper does this as a post-processing layer. (f) Per-carrier (freight) acceptance/rejection rate, on-time-delivery rate, no-show rate. All expressible as beava count, velocity, distance, rate, distribution primitives.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Mixed and heterogeneous within one decision: h3_cell (typically resolution 8-9 for surge, ~0.7-0.1 km^2) cross product_type, driver_id / courier_id / carrier_id, store_id / restaurant_id, rider_id (for cancellation history), (origin_h3 × dest_h3 × hour-of-day) for route-level ETA features, load_id and lane_id for freight. Multiple grains read per decision — a single dispatch evaluates ~5-50 candidate drivers, each requiring per-driver + per-cell + per-route features.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Predominantly sliding / hopping. Uber Gairos's documented set is 6 hop windows from 1 to 32 minutes per H3 cell. DoorDash's published prep-time and store-order-count features are short rolling windows (minutes). Driver-side acceptance/cancellation rates are typically last-N (last 50 offers or 100 trips) or last-K-hours. Exact aggregates are preferred on the surge supply/demand counters (a small error directly distorts the multiplier) but the dispatch pipeline is widely understood to favor freshness and availability over strict consistency — Uber's Marketplace explicitly documents prioritizing data freshness and availability over consistency because late-arriving messages 'don't contribute to the computation' once the decision is made. Approximate (HLL / CMS) sketches are acceptable for n_unique-style features (unique riders served per cell, unique drivers seen in cell) but not for the supply/demand ratio itself.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once with idempotency-by-(event_id) is sufficient and is the de-facto industry standard. Surge / ETA / dispatch are not billing-grade — overcounting one ride request in a hexagon by 1 over 1000 has negligible effect on the multiplier, and the controller re-evaluates every few seconds anyway. The exception is per-driver acceptance / cancellation rate (used for driver-quality scoring and potential deactivation) which is closer to a regulator-visible / driver-livelihood-affecting counter and is typically kept eventually-consistent but auditable upstream in the data warehouse, not in the online feature store.

technical_fit.latency_budget: End-to-end decision budget is the loose target stated in the item description (~100 ms at dispatch); the per-feature read budget is single-digit ms. Uber's own ETA model targets 'single-digit milliseconds' for hundreds of thousands of QPS, and Lyft's published P99 work on online feature serving is at the same tier. Industry guidance (system-design pieces, p99 conf talks) puts P99 dispatch latency under ~300 ms with the actual feature-store hop targeted at sub-25 ms (Redis-class) to sub-ms (Aerospike / in-memory). beava's published sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get is comfortably inside this budget for the feature-read hop.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-minute on the surge / supply-demand side (Uber publicly recomputes surge every few minutes but inputs are aggregated every minute over rolling windows; GoJek computes demand/supply per minute for 44,000 S2ID L13 cells), seconds on the dispatch-feature side (driver online/offline state must propagate within seconds or the optimizer dispatches to a phantom driver), seconds on the restaurant prep-time / store-order-count side (DoorDash explicitly cites the real-time signal on Dasher wait and orders-placed as a top-10 feature for ETA). beava's push-on-event no-broker model fits this tier directly; the alternative incumbents (Kafka + Flink + Redis or Kafka + Flink + DynamoDB) all have one or more hops of latency added compared to direct push.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Per-buyer steady-state EPS is highly variable. Uber globally serves ~10 M ML predictions per second at peak and processes thousands of real-time features for 30 M match-pair predictions per minute; the underlying event rate (ride requests + driver pings + state updates) is at the same order. A driver location-ping at ~4-10 s cadence over 5-10 M concurrent drivers globally is ~0.5-2.5 M EPS just on the supply side. DoorDash processes 'hundreds of billions of events per day' across its real-time event-processing system, putting average EPS in the ~1-3 M range with multiples at peak. Mid-tier regional operators (a regional taxi platform, a single-city delivery operator, a freight broker) are 1-50 k EPS — well inside one beava box at the published ~684 k EPS. Tier-1 (Uber, DoorDash, Lyft, Didi) global aggregate is 10-100x one beava box and requires partitioning that v0 does not ship. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Roughly balanced to read-leaning. Every ride request triggers ~5-50 candidate-driver feature reads plus per-cell surge reads; the write rate (driver pings, state changes, ride events) is also high. Driver-location pings alone make this much more write-heavy than ad-tech frequency capping but more read-heavy than pure telemetry. Net effect: read:write is roughly 2:1 to 10:1 on a typical dispatch decision, strongly favoring beava's batch_get.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Working set is dominated by (h3_cell × product) and per-driver entities. An L8 H3 cell has ~0.7 km^2 area; a tier-1 platform covering ~5,000 active cities times ~10^3-10^4 cells/city = ~10^7 hexes × ~5 product types = ~5×10^7 cell keys at ~200-500 B each (54 features × 6 windows + recency + ratios) ≈ 10-25 GB hot cell state. Plus ~10^7 active drivers globally × ~200-500 B per driver = ~5 GB. Plus ~10^6-10^7 restaurants/stores for delivery × ~500 B = a few GB. Total tier-1 global hot state is on the order of ~30-100 GB, which fits in one beava box but only if all of it is consolidated; regional sharding to one beava box per region (which is the typical real deployment shape — Lyft's online feature store is regional) is more realistic and means per-region hot state is ~5-20 GB, comfortably in-memory. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Bounded-to-slowly-growing on the geographic side (H3 cells are bounded by city footprint; new resolutions / new cities add slowly). Slowly-growing on drivers / restaurants / carriers (millions, not billions; high churn but bounded). Slowly-growing on riders (hundreds of millions; same shape as user_id). Cross products like (origin_h3 × dest_h3 × hour-of-day) are explosive in theory but typically pruned to top-k popular lanes (Uber's DeepETA uses learned embeddings, not exhaustive enumeration). Lower cardinality stress than ad-tech (where (user × campaign) explodes) and much lower than IP / device cardinality in bot defence.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds to days. Per-cell supply/demand windows: 1-32 min sliding; ephemeral. Driver acceptance/cancellation rolling rate: last 50-100 offers, last 7-30 days. Restaurant prep-time: last 10-30 completed orders, last hour. Per-route ETA-error: weeks (slow-changing road conditions, traffic patterns by hour-of-day). Driver / restaurant lifetime stats (used for trust/quality scoring): months to years but typically materialized in the warehouse, not the online store.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20-100+ features per dispatch decision. Uber publicly states dispatch evaluates 'thousands of real-time features' across 30 M match-pair predictions per minute, but per individual (rider, driver) pair the feature vector is in the few-tens-to-low-hundreds range (per-cell supply/demand pair, per-driver score, per-route ETA features, surge multiplier inputs, plus categorical embeddings). Strongly favors batch_get; the canonical pattern is one batch_get per request returning the full per-decision feature vector.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe rather than regulator-grade. Surge / dispatch state can be reconstructed from the Kafka / Kinesis upstream within a minute or two if the online store is lost, because the windows are short (1-32 min) and source-of-truth is the event log; the cost of a brief outage is a few minutes of degraded surge or slightly worse dispatch decisions, not a regulatory finding. beava's WAL + periodic snapshot is the right shape but cold-start replay time on a regional ~10-20 GB hot state is the open question; in practice operators tolerate a 1-2 min warm-up window after a node restart on a regional dispatch box. [uncertain]
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Regional cluster is the dominant deployment shape — Lyft's online feature store is regional with a ValKey write-through cache over DynamoDB; Uber runs Gairos as a regional service per Aurora-style data center; DoorDash's Riviera is multi-region. Single-binary-per-region is a credible v0 fit for mid-size operators (regional taxi platforms, single-country delivery operators, mid-market freight brokers, the long tail of Convoy-Platform-style broker SaaS). Multi-region active-active with consistent counters across regions is NOT required because mobility events are inherently geo-local — a ride request in San Francisco does not need to read a feature from a Tokyo cell — so single-region single-binary is actually a better fit here than for ad-tech frequency capping. The hard v0 limit (no in-process sharding) bites only at tier-1 single-region scale (Uber-SF, DoorDash-NYC-metro).

commercial_fit.who_buys: Marketplace / dispatch / ML platform engineering teams at: (a) ride-hailing operators (Uber, Lyft, Bolt, Didi, Grab, GoJek, Cabify, Yandex Go, inDriver, Curb, Free Now, Ola), (b) on-demand food / grocery / convenience delivery (DoorDash, Instacart, Deliveroo, Zomato, Swiggy, Wolt, Glovo, Rappi, iFood, Uber Eats), (c) digital freight brokers and load boards (Uber Freight, DAT/Convoy Platform, Loadsmart, Flexport, Truckstop, Loadlink), (d) on-demand logistics / last-mile platforms (Shipt, Postmates-legacy, Gopuff, GoPuff-style q-commerce), (e) the long tail of regional / vertical mobility platforms (regional taxi white-labels, mid-size delivery aggregators, B2B trucking marketplaces, micromobility operators like Lime/Bird with dispatch-adjacent supply rebalancing). Buyer persona is typically marketplace engineering / dispatch engineering / ML platform — not the city operations / pricing team who configure rules above the feature layer.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Ride-hailing alone is ~$47-182 B in 2025 depending on definition (Grand View Research $47.6 B; Statista $163-182 B; multiple analysts project $400-800 B by 2032-2035 at 13-19% CAGR). Global food delivery is roughly the same order ($150-300 B). Digital freight brokerage adds another ~$50-100 B. Total addressable mobility-dispatch software / infra layer is the smaller silicon-layer slice of this — order ~$5-20 B in dedicated marketplace / dispatch / pricing infrastructure spend across these operators, dominated today by in-house Kafka+Flink+Redis+DynamoDB stacks plus commercial feature stores (Tecton, Databricks, Vertex AI). The infrastructure savings argument (replace Kafka+Flink+Redis with a single binary) plausibly maps to ~30-70% TCO reduction for mid-market operators based on Criteo / DoorDash-adjacent migrations. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) Cost pressure post-2023: ride-hailing and delivery operators are under shareholder pressure to reach contribution-margin profitability; cutting the dispatch / pricing infrastructure stack from a multi-tier Kafka+Flink+Redis to a single binary is directly accretive. 2) Driver-supply tightening: regulatory wage floors (Seattle, NYC, EU Platform Work Directive 2024) make dispatch quality more valuable per ride — better per-driver acceptance/cancellation features translate to lower deadhead and higher driver utilization. 3) Quick-commerce / instant-delivery wave: every regional q-commerce / dark-store operator (Gopuff, GetirSAB, Flink, Zapp, Blinkit) is greenfield-building a dispatch stack in 2024-2026 and is in scope for a permissively-licensed alternative. 4) Convoy collapse (Oct-2023) and acquihires in 2025: the freight-broker tech vacuum has the second wave of digital brokers (DAT-Convoy, Loadsmart, J.B. Hunt 360) rebuilding matching stacks. 5) Autonomous-vehicle rollouts (Waymo, Cruise-resumed, Zoox): rider-pool optimization, dispatch and remote operations all need real-time per-vehicle features. 6) The Uber / Lyft / DoorDash blog footprint itself is creating expectations among engineering teams at smaller operators that 'sub-ms feature store + H3 surge' is the table-stakes pattern.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Looser than fraud / AML / payments but still real: GDPR / CCPA / state-privacy on rider, driver and courier PII (location, identity) — retention windows for raw location are typically 12-24 months at the operator and weeks-to-months in online features. NYC TLC and similar regulators audit per-driver acceptance / cancellation / utilization rates for license enforcement, so the feature must be auditable upstream (in the warehouse) even if eventually-consistent online. EU AI Act (effective phases 2025-2026) classifies driver / courier scoring as 'high-risk AI' in some readings, which raises explainability requirements on dispatch features. EU Platform Work Directive 2024 explicitly requires algorithmic-management transparency to gig workers, which forces operators to expose what features drive dispatch decisions — a feature store with clear primitive names is operationally easier than opaque Flink jobs. PCI / HIPAA / SOX do not apply. beava's v0 lack of TLS / auth is still a blocker for any production-VPN-exposed deployment.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast for the demo: a runnable H3-cell rolling-demand + per-driver acceptance-rate demo on synthetic event data is a 1-3 day build (declare @bv.event for ride_request / driver_state / offer_response, @bv.table(key=(h3_cell, product)) and @bv.table(key=driver_id), seed events, batch_get). 2-6 weeks to a credible pilot at a mid-market operator once TLS / auth / regional-deployment story is in place. 3-9 months to displace a Kafka+Flink+Redis production stack at a regional ride-hailing or delivery operator; longer at tier-1 because of internal-tooling and observability investments around the existing stack.

competition.incumbents: (a) In-house Kafka + Flink + Redis is the dominant pattern at every tier-1 operator: Uber Gairos (Flink + Pinot + custom storage), DoorDash Riviera (Flink + Kafka + Redis feature store), Lyft (Flink + Beam + DynamoDB + ValKey), Instacart Griffin (Kafka + stream processing + custom serving), GoJek Feast (originated at GoJek, now LF AI). (b) Commercial feature stores: Tecton (positions for dispatch / fraud / personalization at large operators), Chalk (real-time feature platform with declarative DSL), Featureform (open-source feature store wrapper), Hopsworks, Fennel, Feast (open-source, originally GoJek). (c) Stream-processing engines plus serving stores: Flink, Spark Structured Streaming, RisingWave, Materialize for the streaming layer; Redis / Aerospike / DynamoDB / ScyllaDB / DragonflyDB for the online store. (d) Geospatial-aware streaming: Druid (used at Lyft for analytics), Pinot (used at Uber for Gairos), TimescaleDB, ClickHouse (with H3 / geohash UDFs). beava's competitive surface in this domain is mostly versus 'in-house Redis + Flink' (the most common DIY shape) and versus Tecton / Fennel for greenfield builds.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific incumbents are mostly internal stacks rather than vendor products: Uber's Gairos + Michelangelo + DeepETA (in-house), DoorDash's DeepRed + Riviera (in-house), Lyft's Feature Store with dsfeatures wrapper (in-house, Apache Beam + Flink + DynamoDB + ValKey), GoJek's Jaeger dispatch + Surbo surge + Feast (some open-sourced), Grab and Bolt mostly internal. On the vendor side: Tecton has marketed dispatch / mobility use cases in conference talks (and Tecton's examples repo includes a ride-hailing-style streaming demo), Chalk pitches at the same tier, Aerospike has Swiggy as a public dispatch / feature-store customer. Open-source projects with mobility-shaped demos: Feast (GoJek-originated), Apache Pinot (Uber-originated, real-time OLAP, used for Gairos), Apache Hudi (Uber-originated). No incumbent owns the 'single-binary regional dispatch feature server' niche that beava could plausibly own.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single binary replaces the (Kafka producer + Flink job + Redis / DynamoDB online store + serving layer) chain — meaningful for the regional / mid-market operator who can't afford a 4-component stack. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives directly express the count / velocity / rate / distribution / distance feature shapes the domain documents publicly (Gairos's 54 features per hex per minute IS exactly this primitive set). 3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get matches the dispatch P99 budget. 4) Apache-2.0, no open-core — meaningful versus Tecton SaaS lock-in and versus the operational burden of Flink + Redis Enterprise. 5) Push-on-event model fits the dispatcher / pricing-controller-emits-events shape natively (driver pings, ride requests, offers, completions are already events) — no Kafka broker round-trip required for the inline pipeline. 6) H3 / geohash / S2 cells are just composite primary keys to beava's @bv.table — no special geospatial-index infrastructure needed. 7) Per-key TTL + window semantics built-in means rolling acceptance/cancellation/idle-time features need no custom Lua / UDF. 8) The mid-market operator who today runs 'Postgres + nightly Airflow + cron + a hand-rolled Redis cache' for dispatch features can leapfrog to streaming without adopting Flink.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth — disqualifying for any production deployment outside a tightly-controlled VPC; operators run dispatch features alongside rider/driver PII (location, IDs) and cannot expose unauthenticated push/admin surfaces. 2) No geospatial indices — H3 / S2 / geohash cells are just opaque string/int keys to beava; queries like 'all hexes within ring(7) of cell X' must be computed by the caller from H3 library and issued as a batch_get list, not as a server-side ring query. Uber's Gairos publicly indexes by H3 ring at the server. 3) No in-process sharding — single-binary v0 is fine for a regional operator but does not consolidate a multi-region operator. 4) No first-class streaming join / lookup — features like 'when this driver-offer arrives, fetch driver's last-N acceptance rate AND the cell's current supply/demand' are clean in beava as parallel batch_gets but materialized streaming joins (Flink SQL) win on more complex enrichment. 5) No native triggers — surge pricing wants 'fire when supply/demand ratio in cell X crosses 1.2' as a callback for fast-path multiplier updates, not as a poll. 6) Limited geospatial primitives — Uber-style H3 ring aggregation (resolution 8, ring radii 0/1/2/3/4/5/10/15/20) requires the caller to enumerate cells in the ring; the alternative incumbents (Pinot with H3 indexes, Druid with geohash indexes) push this server-side. 7) No public mobility / dispatch case study yet. 8) Cold-start replay time on a regional 10-20 GB hot dispatch state is unbenchmarked. [uncertain] 9) No built-in driver-livelihood / regulatory-audit retention (per-driver feature history with auditable retention windows) — operators have to keep that in a separate warehouse anyway, but it's not a v0 affordance.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: rider app (HTTP/JSON :8080 for ride_request and cancel events), driver app (TCP+msgpack :8081 for ~4-10 s location pings to handle the high write rate), dispatcher service (gRPC or TCP for offer/accept/decline events), restaurant POS / merchant integration for prep-time and queue-depth events, freight TMS / carrier API for tender events. Consumers: dispatcher / matching service reading via batch_get on every request; surge / pricing controller polling per-cell features every few seconds; ETA service reading per-route + per-store features synchronously on quote; driver-quality scoring batch job (offline). The HTTP+TCP push surface fits a mobility operator's already-event-driven internal architecture better than a Kafka-only feature store like Feast (which would require running Kafka + connectors). The main integration gap is the typical operator already runs Kafka for warehouse / lakehouse / observability, so beava would coexist with Kafka rather than replace it — push directly from the dispatcher AND fan-out from Kafka via a thin shim.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. Surge multiplier is a rules-engine plus model — typically a piecewise function over the supply/demand ratio (Uber publicly documents a threshold around ~1.2 ratio) potentially blended with a learned multiplier model. Dispatch matching is an optimization solver (Hungarian / mixed-integer / heuristic in DeepRed) fed by ML-scored per-pair predictions (Uber's tree-based + ensembling per match-pair). ETA is pure ML (DeepETA's transformer encoder-decoder, DoorDash's gradient-boosting with real-time features). beava sits below all three and exposes the same per-entity primitives — surge controller reads counters directly, dispatch optimizer reads features that feed a sidecar XGBoost / ONNX scorer, ETA service reads features that feed a Tensorflow / PyTorch model in a separate process.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public beava users in mobility / dispatch yet. [uncertain] Comparable production systems with extensive public documentation: Uber Gairos (Apache Flink + custom storage; 54 features per H3 hex per minute via 9 rings × 6 window sizes), Uber DeepETA (single-digit ms inference, hundreds of thousands of QPS), DoorDash Riviera + DeepRed (declarative YAML-DSL feature framework over Flink; store-order-count and dasher-wait features in top-10 for ETA), Lyft (Apache Beam + Flink + DynamoDB + ValKey LRU cache; regional online feature store; P99 work documented at p99 conf), Instacart Griffin (Kafka + stream processing + unified feature interface), GoJek (Surbo surge over 44,000 S2 L13 cells per minute, ~1 M data points/min peak, Jaeger multi-objective dispatch, originated Feast), Swiggy (Aerospike-backed real-time feature store, public AWS / Aerospike case study), AWS RTB-adjacent and dispatch-adjacent reference architectures. The Tecton examples repo includes a ride-hailing-style streaming demo, and Featureform / Hopsworks both pitch dispatch use cases but without named tier-1 customers.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion / RFC threads on mobility / dispatch / surge identified in this snapshot. [uncertain] Adjacent active community signals: Uber Engineering blog series on Gairos, DeepETA, surge pricing and H3 (h3geo.org / github.com/uber/h3 — active OSS community, MIT-licensed), DoorDash Engineering blog (Riviera, DeepRed, Building A Declarative Real-Time Feature Engineering Framework), Lyft Engineering blog and p99 conf talks (Taming P99 Latencies at Lyft), GoJek / Gojek Tech blog (Surbo, Feast), Instacart 'Lessons Learned: Journey to Real-Time Machine Learning', Apache Flink / Beam community channels, the Feature Store for ML community (featurestore.org), arXiv pacing / dispatch / ETA papers including DeeprETA (2206.02127).
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No mobility / dispatch demo ships in beava v0. Existing demos under /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ are adtech, ecommerce and fraud only. A first runnable mobility demo would declare @bv.event for RideRequest / DriverState / Offer / RideComplete and @bv.table aggregations keyed by (h3_cell, product_type) and driver_id — a one-to-two-afternoon authoring effort, structurally similar to the existing adtech demo. [uncertain] This is a gap to fill before pitching mobility buyers; the absence of a dispatch demo is conspicuous given the README explicitly lists 'Redis for stateful streaming features' positioning that maps directly to this domain.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Low to moderate. Riders, drivers and couriers occasionally game incentives (driver-side surge-chasing, position-spoofing, fake cancellations) but the headline domain is not adversary-driven the way fraud or bot defence is. The 'pressure' is operational: scale (10^7-10^8 events / day per region), tight latency (~100 ms decision budget), high write rate from continuous driver pings, and the cost of a stale or wrong feature (a misdirected dispatch is a bad customer experience but not a regulatory finding). Driver-quality scoring features have some adversarial pressure (drivers learn to game acceptance/cancellation thresholds) but it's slower-moving than card-fraud adversary cycles.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Long-historical lookback for ETA model training — that is a lakehouse / Parquet / data-warehouse job (Hudi, Iceberg, Delta) and not a beava job. beava feeds online inference, not training. 2) Geospatial joins ('all drivers within 2 km of cell X', 'all stores within ring(3) of rider's cell') — beava does not have a geospatial index; the caller must enumerate cells client-side and issue batch_get. For server-side ring / radius queries the buyer keeps an H3-aware OLAP layer (Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse with H3 UDFs). 3) The dispatch optimizer itself — beava is the feature backend underneath the optimizer (DeepRed / Jaeger / Hungarian-matching), not the optimizer. 4) Multi-region active-active counter consistency — not actually required for mobility (geo-local events) so this is a non-issue rather than a gap. 5) Acting as the system of record for driver / rider / carrier identity, payouts, ratings — those live in OLTP / data-warehouse systems upstream. 6) Long retention for regulatory driver-stat audits — operators keep that in the warehouse. 7) Generative-AI / LLM dispatch features (the 2024+ Michelangelo generative push) — beava is for tabular streaming features, not LLM context. 8) Cross-entity OLAP joins ('top 100 cells by demand for product Comfort across all cities last hour') — that is a Pinot / Druid query.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for mobility / dispatch, in rough priority order: 1) TLS termination and token / mTLS auth on :8081 / :8090 — without this, operators cannot deploy beava in any production VPC that touches rider/driver PII or location. 2) An H3 / S2 / geohash-aware @bv.table key helper and a server-side ring / k-ring batch_get primitive (or at minimum, a documented client recipe using uber/h3 and a single batch_get over the enumerated cell list) — this is the single biggest 'dispatch-shaped' DX gap. 3) In-process sharding by entity-key prefix so a tier-1 single-region (Uber-SF, DoorDash-Manhattan) can scale within one cluster without external hand-sharding. 4) Triggers / 'callback when counter crosses threshold' for surge multiplier transitions and for low-supply / high-demand alerting; today the surge controller has to poll. 5) Multi-tenancy (per-tenant namespaces, per-tenant quotas) for SaaS dispatch / freight-broker / fleet-management vendors who want to embed beava per-customer. 6) A bounded WAL-replay-time SLA for ~10-50 GB regional dispatch state — a node restart during evening peak must not become an outage. 7) A documented mobility / dispatch reference architecture and a vertical demo in /python/beava/demos/ covering (a) H3 supply/demand per minute over (1,2,4,8,16,32) min windows, (b) per-driver acceptance/cancellation/idle-time rolling features, (c) per-restaurant prep-time velocity, (d) per-(origin × dest × hour) ETA-error rolling stats. 8) A streaming-side admin / debug surface ('top-k cells by surge multiplier right now', 'top-k drivers by recent cancellation rate') without materializing the full keyspace. 9) Optional integration with Kafka / Kinesis as a fan-in source so operators who already run Kafka can mirror dispatch events into beava without rewiring producers. 10) Per-key retention with explicit policy hooks for GDPR / EU Platform Work Directive driver-data deletion. 11) A documented driver-quality / acceptance-rate feature pattern that distinguishes online (real-time, eventually-consistent) from the regulator-grade audit history (which stays in the warehouse).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — surge pricing is fundamentally a threshold-crossing controller ('when supply/demand ratio in cell X crosses 1.2, raise multiplier; when it drops, lower it'). Today an operator polls per-cell features every few seconds from a separate pricing controller (the Gairos / Surbo pattern). A first-class threshold-trigger primitive in beava would let the controller run as a callback rather than a poll, which is meaningful at scale (10^4-10^7 hexes per operator). Dispatch matching does NOT need triggers — the feature read happens on every offer anyway — but surge transitions, low-supply alerts, and ETA-error drift detection all do.
